title: I Gave My Last $20 to a Soldier on Christmas Eve. A Year LATER...

scenes.text: Sweetheart, on Christmas Eve of nineteen sixty-nine, I had exactly twenty dollars in my purse. It was all the money we had for Christmas dinner and the children's presents. And in the Greyhound station in Mansfield, at eleven o'clock at night, I gave every penny of it to a young soldier I had never seen before in my life. My husband didn't speak to me for two days.
scenes.query: 1960s Greyhound bus station at night
scenes.caption: MY LAST TWENTY DOLLARS

scenes.text: Tonight I'm going to tell you why I did it, what that soldier said to me, and what pulled up in front of our house exactly one year later, on Christmas Eve of nineteen seventy. Stay with me, honey, because I didn't believe it myself until I saw his face. And I still keep what he left on my kitchen table.
scenes.query: car pulling up to house in snow night
scenes.caption: ONE YEAR LATER

scenes.text: That was a hard year for us, sweetheart. Harold had been laid off from the plant in October, and he was working odd jobs, shoveling snow and fixing furnaces for cash. We had two little ones, Susan and Mark, five and three. I was taking in sewing. Every week, we counted every penny on the kitchen table, and every week there were fewer of them.
scenes.query: 1960s couple counting money at kitchen table
scenes.caption: COUNTING EVERY PENNY

scenes.text: By Christmas Eve, I had saved twenty dollars in an envelope in my sewing box. Twenty dollars, honey. In nineteen sixty-nine, that was a ham, a sack of potatoes, a pie, a doll for Susan, and a little red fire truck for Mark that I'd had my eye on at the five-and-dime for two months. I had it all planned to the penny.
scenes.query: red toy fire truck in store window 1960s
scenes.caption: PLANNED TO THE PENNY

scenes.text: But on Christmas Eve, my mother called. My father had fallen on the ice and broken his hip, and she needed me at the hospital in Columbus. Harold stayed with the children, and I took the evening bus with my envelope in my purse, because I planned to shop at the big stores on the way home. In a minute I'll tell you why I never got to those stores.
scenes.query: woman boarding bus in snow evening
scenes.caption: THE EVENING BUS

scenes.text: My father was all right, thank the Lord. On the way home, I had to change buses in Mansfield, and the station was nearly empty. Just me, an old man asleep on a bench, and a boy in an army uniform sitting by himself in the corner, with a duffel bag between his feet. He was crying, honey. Trying hard not to, the way young men do. But crying.
scenes.query: young soldier alone in bus station crying
scenes.caption: A BOY IN UNIFORM

scenes.text: I'm a mother. I couldn't stand it. So I went over and sat down next to him and said, son, are you all right? He wiped his face fast and said, yes, ma'am, I'm fine. And then he told me everything, all at once, the way people do with strangers at midnight. His name was Billy. He was nineteen. And he had just gotten home from Vietnam.
scenes.query: woman sitting next to young soldier bench
scenes.caption: HIS NAME WAS BILLY

scenes.text: He'd been wounded in the leg in October, and he'd spent two months in an army hospital. They'd let him go home for Christmas. But somewhere between California and Ohio, somebody had stolen his wallet while he slept on the bus. All his money. His ticket to Akron, where his mother and little sisters lived. And the last bus to Akron left in forty minutes.
scenes.query: soldier searching empty duffel bag
scenes.caption: HIS WALLET WAS STOLEN

scenes.text: He said, I called my mom from the pay phone, collect. She doesn't have the money either. She's been working two jobs since my dad died. I told her I'd make it home somehow. And then he said, I promised her, ma'am. I promised her I'd be home for Christmas, every letter I wrote from over there. That's what kept me going. And now I'm going to break it.
scenes.query: pay phone in bus station 1960s
scenes.caption: I PROMISED HER

scenes.text: If you're enjoying Grandma's story, tap the like button for me, sweetheart. It helps more people find these stories. I sat there with my purse on my lap and my hand on that envelope. Twenty dollars. The ham. The doll. The red fire truck. I thought about Harold. I thought about my babies' faces on Christmas morning with nothing under the tree. And then I thought about Billy's mother.
scenes.query: hand on purse with envelope
scenes.caption: I THOUGHT ABOUT HIS MOTHER

scenes.text: I opened my purse, took out the envelope, and put the whole thing in his hand. The ticket to Akron was four dollars and ten cents. I said, Billy, buy your ticket. And use the rest to bring something home to your mother and your sisters. He tried to give it back. He said, ma'am, I can't. I can tell this is a lot of money to you. And I said, it's Christmas, son. Go home.
scenes.query: woman giving envelope to soldier
scenes.caption: IT'S CHRISTMAS, SON. GO HOME.

scenes.text: He asked for my name and address. He said, I'm going to pay you back, every penny. And I wrote it on the back of his bus ticket, but I didn't expect a thing, honey. I watched him limp out to that bus with his duffel bag, and he turned around at the door and saluted me. A real salute. And then the bus pulled away into the snow.
scenes.query: soldier saluting at bus door in snow
scenes.caption: HE SALUTED ME

scenes.text: I walked home from the station with an empty purse, and I cried the whole way. Not because I was sorry. Because I was scared. When I got home and told Harold, he didn't yell. That was worse, sweetheart. He just went quiet. He said, Ruth, what are we going to tell the children? And he went to bed without another word.
scenes.query: woman walking alone in snow at night
scenes.caption: WHAT DO WE TELL THEM?

scenes.text: Christmas morning, there was nothing under our tree but two oranges and a pair of mittens I'd knitted for each child. We had pancakes for Christmas dinner, honey. Pancakes and the last of the maple syrup. Mark didn't understand. He kept asking where Santa was. Susan understood. She was five, and she patted my hand and said, Mommy, I like pancakes best anyway.
scenes.query: pancakes on plate simple Christmas
scenes.caption: PANCAKES FOR CHRISTMAS

scenes.text: And then, around noon, there was a knock at the door. It was Mr. Kowalski from next door, with a ham. And then the Johnsons from across the street, with a pie. And Pastor Gray, with a bag of toys from the church. I never told anybody what happened. To this day, I think Susan went next door and told Mrs. Kowalski. That little girl. She never would admit it.
scenes.query: neighbors bringing food to door Christmas
scenes.caption: THE NEIGHBORS CAME

scenes.text: So far, the station, the envelope, the salute, and the pancakes. Harold forgave me by New Year's. He said, Ruthie, I'd have done the same thing. I'd have just felt worse about it. Life went on. Harold got called back to the plant in March. Things got better. And I didn't hear one word from Billy. Not a letter, not a card. Nothing.
scenes.query: mailbox empty winter
scenes.caption: NOT ONE WORD

scenes.text: Harold's brother said, you'll never see that money again, Ruth. Every soldier in every bus station has a sad story. I'd bet you he was drinking it up in a bar in Akron an hour later. And I'll admit, honey, as the months went by, a little part of me started to wonder if he was right. Not about the money. About Billy.
scenes.query: skeptical man at kitchen table
scenes.caption: HE WAS PROBABLY LYING

scenes.text: On Christmas Eve of nineteen seventy, exactly one year later, at seven o'clock at night, a car pulled up in front of our house on Maple Drive. A blue station wagon. Susan was at the window, and she said, Mommy, there's a soldier. And my heart stopped. Because walking up our front steps, limping just a little, in his dress uniform, was Billy.
scenes.query: soldier in dress uniform walking up snowy steps
scenes.caption: MOMMY, THERE'S A SOLDIER

scenes.text: And he wasn't alone. Behind him came a little woman in a church coat, his mother, and three teenage girls, his sisters, all carrying boxes. Billy stood at our door, took off his cap, and said, Mrs. Miller, I'm sorry it took me a year. I wanted to do it right. And then his mother pushed right past him and threw her arms around my neck and wouldn't let go.
scenes.query: mother hugging woman at door Christmas
scenes.caption: TO DO IT RIGHT

scenes.text: She said, you brought my boy home for Christmas. Do you know what that meant? His father died the year before he shipped out. I'd prayed every night for two years that he'd come through that door again. And on Christmas morning, there he was, with a box of chocolates and a bottle of perfume, and a little doll for each of his sisters. He told me a lady at the bus station gave it to him.
scenes.query: family reunion soldier Christmas morning
scenes.caption: YOU BROUGHT MY BOY HOME

scenes.text: The boxes, sweetheart. A ham, the biggest one I've ever seen. Two pies his mother had baked. A doll for Susan with a blue dress. And for Mark, a red toy fire truck. Not the little one from the five-and-dime. A big metal one, with a ladder that went up and a bell that rang. Mark rang that bell until Harold hid it in the closet in February.
scenes.query: big red metal toy fire truck with ladder
scenes.caption: A RED FIRE TRUCK

scenes.text: And then Billy handed me an envelope. A plain white envelope, just like mine. Inside was a twenty-dollar bill, and a letter. He'd gotten a job at the tire factory in Akron when he got out. He said he'd put aside one dollar every two weeks, all year, in a coffee can, so it would be his own money that paid me back, not a check. He wanted it to be real.
scenes.query: envelope with twenty dollar bill and letter
scenes.caption: ONE DOLLAR AT A TIME

scenes.text: Then he stood up straight and said, Mrs. Miller, I was sitting in that station thinking about whether it was even worth going home. I'd seen some things over there. I didn't think I could be a regular person anymore. And then a stranger gave me everything she had. I figured if people like you are out here, then it's worth being home. I've never forgotten those words, sweetheart. Not one.
scenes.query: young veteran speaking emotionally
scenes.caption: IT'S WORTH BEING HOME

scenes.text: Billy and his family came every Christmas Eve for twenty-two years, honey. He married a girl named Carol, became a foreman at the tire factory, and had four children. When Harold passed, Billy was a pallbearer. And when Billy passed, in two thousand fifteen, his oldest son called me. He said, Mrs. Miller, Dad asked that you have this. It was the bus ticket, honey. My address still on the back.
scenes.query: old bus ticket with handwriting
scenes.caption: THE BUS TICKET

scenes.text: I still have that twenty-dollar bill, sweetheart. I never spent it. It's in a frame on my kitchen wall, next to the bus ticket, and the letter. Every Christmas Eve, I take it down and read the letter out loud to my grandchildren. And I tell them what I'm telling you. The best twenty dollars you'll ever spend is the twenty you can't afford to give.
scenes.query: framed twenty dollar bill on kitchen wall
scenes.caption: THE BEST TWENTY DOLLARS

scenes.text: Tell me in the comments, honey. Would you have given away your last twenty dollars on Christmas Eve? Be honest with Grandma. And if you or someone you love served, I want to thank them. There are more of my family's stories in the playlist right there on your screen, and I'll see you in the next one. Good night, sweetheart. Merry Christmas.
scenes.query: small house with Christmas lights in snow
scenes.caption: WOULD YOU HAVE GIVEN IT?
